walkthroughs.title: 2022: the rate bear
steps: Inflation was running hot. Prices were up 9.1% in the year to June 2022, the most since 1981.
The Fed started the year near zero. Seven hikes later it ended at 4.25% to 4.50%.
The S&P 500 went from 4,796.56 on January 3 to 3,577.03 on October 12. About a quarter of its value, gone.

walkthroughs.title: How a bottom forms
steps: A bottom is a process, not a day. And it forms in fear and bad headlines, not in clarity.
First the panic. Capitulation, the VIX spiking, a washout where almost nothing holds its 50-day.
Then the turn. Bad news stops working, a follow-through day fires, and new leaders break out.
No one signpost proves it. I want to see several of them line up.

walkthroughs.title: Confirm, don't predict
steps: Don't try to call the bottom. O'Neil's way is to wait until a new uptrend has already started.
The tell is a follow-through day. Several days into a rally attempt, a major index rises strongly on higher volume.
It's not foolproof. About half to two-thirds of them lead to a lasting uptrend.
When it fires, look at the strongest stocks first. They're usually the first ones out.

questions.q: Everyone on TV says we're "in a bear market" now. What does that label actually mean?
choices: A drop of 20% or more from a high
A drop of 10% from a recent high
Three lower weekly closes in a row
The Fed raising interest rates
questions.answer: A drop of 20% or more from a high
questions.why: Down 20% or more from the high. That's the usual line for a broad index, and the drop has to last at least two months. A 10% drop is what most people call a correction. Know the label, but don't trade off it. The 20% line is a convention, not a signal. Nobody rings a bell at minus 20%, and I'm not buying or selling because an index crossed it. I'm watching what price and the leaders do.
questions.lesson_line: Minus 20% makes it a bear on paper. It's a label, not a signal.

wrong.A drop of 10% from a recent high: That's a correction, the smaller drop. The bear label starts at 20%.
wrong.Three lower weekly closes in a row: Made-up rule. The label is about how far a broad index falls, 20% or more.
wrong.The Fed raising interest rates: Rate hikes can help bring a bear on. The label itself is about how far prices fall.

questions.simple: A bear market is a broad index down 20% or more from its high. It's a label, not a signal to trade.

reasons: stable definition: one Tier 1 fact plus an agreeing Tier 2 fact

questions.q: Someone in the chat says the market "just capitulated." What are they describing?
choices: Panic selling that speeds up the fall
Big buyers stepping in at the low
A slow drift lower on light volume
The first big up day off the market low
questions.answer: Panic selling that speeds up the fall
questions.why: Panic selling. Capitulation is the crowd giving up. People who held all the way down finally dump, and the drop gets faster, not slower. On the chart you'll see big red bars on unusually heavy volume. Here's why I care. That panic is how a washout starts, the first step of a bottom. It's rarely the low itself, so I'm not buying it. I mark it and watch what comes next.
questions.lesson_line: Capitulation is the crowd giving up. Fast, loud, heavy volume. It starts a bottom. It's rarely the bottom.

wrong.Big buyers stepping in at the low: That's the other side of the trade. Big buyers soak up the panic, but the panic itself is the capitulation.
wrong.A slow drift lower on light volume: That's the opposite. Capitulation is fast and loud, sharp drops on unusually high volume.
wrong.The first big up day off the market low: That's the bounce that can come after. Capitulation is the selling before it.

questions.simple: Capitulation is panic selling, the crowd giving up, and it makes a falling market drop even faster.

questions.q: On a day the S&P 500 sells off hard, the VIX usually jumps.
questions.why: True. The VIX is the market's read on how much the S&P 500 will swing over the next 30 days. It comes from option prices. People call it the Fear Index. When stocks fall fast, panic hits, option prices jump, and the VIX spikes. So the two most often move opposite each other. Put the VIX next to the S&P 500 on any ugly day and you'll see it. I use it as a fear gauge. It's not a timing tool.
questions.lesson_line: Stocks down hard, VIX up. It's a fear gauge, not a timing tool.
questions.simple: True. When stocks drop hard, fear jumps, and the VIX measures that fear through option prices.

questions.q: The index just made a new low, but fewer stocks went with it this time. What do you call that?
questions.sentence: Index at a new low, fewer stocks at new lows than last time. That's a bullish ___.
questions.why: Divergence. The index broke to a new low, but the stocks underneath didn't follow it down. Fewer made new lows than last time. Breadth is just how many stocks take part in a move. Here breadth is improving while the index looks worse. The selling is getting narrower. I treat that as a clue a turn could be coming. It's not proof until price backs it up, so I build my list and wait.
questions.lesson_line: Look under the index. A new low most stocks skip is a bullish divergence.
questions.simple: Divergence. The index made a new low, but fewer stocks went with it, and that can come before a turn up.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Capitulation shows up as a sharp drop on unusually heavy ___.
questions.why: Volume. Investopedia says traders look for unusually high trading volume with sharp price drops to signal capitulation. ChartSchool's Wyckoff tutorial shows the selling climax the same way: wide price ranges and heavy volume. On that day price often closes well off the low, as large buyers absorb the selling.
questions.lesson_line: Big drop, huge volume, a close well off the low. That's the look of a washout.
questions.simple: Volume, because panic selling shows up as a huge number of shares traded on a sharp drop.

questions.q: The market's been falling for months and you're itching to buy. In O'Neil's method, what is the follow-through day for?
choices: Confirm the new uptrend
Call the exact bottom day
Signal a short on the bounce
Mark the top of the rally
questions.why: Confirming the new uptrend. O'Neil's whole point was don't try to call the bottom. Wait until the market shows you a new uptrend has started. The follow-through day is that proof. It most often comes several days into a rally attempt, when a major index rises strongly on higher volume. The volume is the tell. It says big institutions are stepping back in. You give up the first part of the move off the low. In exchange you're not catching falling knives.
questions.lesson_line: Don't guess the bottom. Let the market prove a new uptrend has started.

wrong.Signal a short on the bounce: It's a buy-side signal. It says big buyers are starting to step back in.
wrong.Call the exact bottom day: It comes several days after the low, not on it. The whole point is to stop guessing the bottom.
wrong.Mark the top of the rally: It shows up early in a new uptrend, a few days off a low, not at a top.

questions.simple: It confirms a new uptrend has started, so you buy into proof instead of guessing the bottom.

questions.q: A follow-through day means the market's low is in for good.
questions.why: False. A follow-through day shifts the odds. It doesn't lock in the low. IBD itself says these signals aren't foolproof. One StockCharts writer cites studies of past cycles: about half to two-thirds lead to a lasting uptrend. So plenty fail. That's why you start with a few of your best names, not the whole list. Each one gets a real stop with the broker. If they work, you take more names. If they fail, you're out small and mostly in cash.
questions.lesson_line: A follow-through day shifts the odds. It doesn't promise you the low.
questions.simple: False. Some follow-through days fail and the market rolls back over, so it shifts the odds without promising anything.

reasons: the success-rate figure rests on one article citing unnamed studies (the key does not)

questions.q: On a huge-volume flush, you can confirm capitulation the same day it happens.
questions.why: False. You only know it was capitulation after it's over and price has bounced back. Bear markets throw several big-volume plunges at you, and people call capitulation early, and wrong, more than once. Even a real washout is where the bottoming starts. It's rarely the low itself. So on the day, I don't buy the flush. I mark its low, then wait to see if the low holds and a rally gets going.
questions.lesson_line: Capitulation gets named in hindsight. On the day, mark it and wait.
questions.simple: False. You only know it was capitulation after it ends and prices bounce back.

questions.q: The S&P 500 closed at 4,796.56 on Jan. 3, 2022 and 3,577.03 on Oct. 12. How deep was that drawdown, peak to low?
questions.why: 25.4%. Work it from the peak. 4,796.56 minus 3,577.03 is 1,219.53. Divide that by the peak, 4,796.56, then times 100. That's 25.4%. You always divide by where it started, not where it ended. These are closing prices, so it's close to close. That's well past the 20% line, and it took most of a year. About a quarter of the index's value, gone.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a drawdown from the peak close. 2022 took about a quarter off the S&P 500.
questions.simple: It fell 25.4%, the drop from 4,796.56 to 3,577.03 divided by the peak.

wrong.34.1%: You divided the drop by the low. A drawdown is measured from the peak.
wrong.74.6%: That's what was left, not what was lost.
wrong.2.54%: Decimal slip. Move it one place and it's 25.4%.

questions.q: You're studying the 2022 bear. What did the Fed do with its target rate range that year?
choices: From near zero to 4.25%-4.50%
From 4.25%-4.50% down to near zero
It held near zero all year
Up to 9.1%, to match inflation
questions.why: Near zero to 4.25%-4.50%. The range sat at 0 to 0.25% from March 2020 until March 2022. Then the Fed hiked at seven meetings in one year, March 17 through Dec. 15. That's the backdrop for the whole 2022 bear. Markets swung hard all year on how badly higher rates would hurt. You don't need to trade the Fed. But know the backdrop, and don't mix the two numbers up. The 9.1% was inflation, not the Fed's rate.
questions.lesson_line: 2022 was a rate bear. The Fed went from near zero to over 4% in one year.

wrong.From 4.25%-4.50% down to near zero: Backwards. Near zero is where 2022 started. 4.25% to 4.50% is where it ended.
wrong.It held near zero all year: It started near zero, then rose fast. Seven hikes in one year.
wrong.Up to 9.1%, to match inflation: 9.1% was inflation, the 12 months to June. The Fed's range ended 2022 at 4.25% to 4.50%.

questions.simple: It went from near zero to 4.25%-4.50%, with seven hikes in one year.

questions.q: In 2022 the Fed hiked by 0.75 point at four straight meetings.
questions.why: True. Three-quarters of a point, 75 basis points, on June 16, July 28, Sept. 22 and Nov. 3. Four in a row, each one triple the usual size. Then a smaller 50 on Dec. 15. That's the Fed hitting the brakes hard. When rates jump that fast, the market spends all year guessing how much damage they'll do. That's where the big swings of 2022 came from, both ways. You don't trade the Fed. But know what the market's fighting, so a fast bounce doesn't fool you.
questions.lesson_line: Four jumbo hikes in a row. That's the pace behind the 2022 bear.
questions.simple: True. The Fed raised rates by 0.75 point at four meetings in a row, June through November.

questions.q: Deep in a bear, the Nasdaq closed at 12,581.22 on March 14, 2022 and 14,619.64 on the 29th. How big was that rally?
questions.why: 16.2%. 14,619.64 minus 12,581.22 is 2,038.42. Divide by the start, 12,581.22, and it's 16.2%. That's a big two weeks, and it felt like the bottom was in. It wasn't. The Nasdaq made new lows four weeks later. That's a bear market rally, sharp and short. It traps people who think the decline is over. You can't know it's one until it fails. So I want a follow-through day and leaders breaking out, not just a fast bounce.
questions.lesson_line: A bear rally can run 16% in two weeks and still fail. Size alone proves nothing.
questions.simple: It rallied 16.2% in about two weeks and still made new lows later, so size alone proves nothing.

deeper.trap: A 16% jump in two weeks can feel like a new bull. Investopedia notes the Nasdaq was already down 22% from the prior year's high when it ran. It set new lows four weeks later. Bear market rallies are sharp and short, and they trap people who think the decline is over.

wrong.13.9%: You divided by the end level. A percent change runs from the start.
wrong.116.2%: That's the ratio. Subtract one to get the gain.

questions.q: The index has been falling hard for weeks. You pull up breadth. Which reading says this is a washout?
choices: Under 15% above their 50-day
Over 70% above their 50-day
Index at a new high, VIX near lows
Volume drying up for a whole week
questions.why: Under 15% of stocks above their 50-day. Almost nothing is holding up. For context, under 30% already counts as oversold, so 15% is deep. That's a washout: panic, extreme fear, a big flush down. It's where the bottoming process starts. It's rarely where the index makes its low. So I don't buy the washout itself. I start working my watch list there and wait for the turn.
questions.lesson_line: A washout means almost nothing is holding up. It starts the bottom. It's rarely the low.

wrong.Over 70% above their 50-day: That's the other end. Above 70% is overbought, not panic.
wrong.Index at a new high, VIX near lows: That's calm, not panic. A washout comes with extreme fear.
wrong.Volume drying up for a whole week: Quiet isn't panic. A washout is a big, scared flush, and capitulation comes on unusually heavy volume.

questions.simple: Under 15% above their 50-day fits, because in a washout almost every stock has broken down.

reasons: the 15% line comes from one source (CMT Association)

questions.q: After weeks of selling, someone says we just got a breadth thrust. What happened?
choices: A burst of broad buying off a low
A few giant stocks lifting the index
A spike in stocks at new lows
A slow grind up on light volume
questions.answer: A burst of broad buying off a low
questions.why: A burst of broad buying off a low. A lot of stocks turned up together, fast. In Zweig's version, the reading swings from below 40% to above 61.5% within 10 days. That's an oversold market turning strong in a hurry, and it's rare. Here's the catch. You can get one or two thrusts inside a bear rally. A run of them rarely shows up before the real low. So one thrust gets my attention. A run of them is what I want to see.
questions.lesson_line: One thrust gets my attention. A run of them is what shows up after a real low.

wrong.A few giant stocks lifting the index: That's narrow, the opposite. An index can rise while most of its stocks fall.
wrong.A spike in stocks at new lows: That's the washout side, the panic before the turn.
wrong.A slow grind up on light volume: A thrust is fast and broad. Light-volume moves count for less.

questions.simple: It's a burst of broad buying, lots of stocks turning up together fast off a low.

questions.story: Day six of a bounce off a fresh low. The Nasdaq's up 1.9% today. Volume came in lighter than yesterday and below average.
questions.q: Is this your follow-through day?
choices: No, volume didn't pick up
Yes, the gain is big enough
Yes, any up day off a low counts
No, it's too late in the bounce
questions.why: No. The price showed up, the volume didn't. A follow-through day needs both: a strong gain in a major index on higher volume. The volume is the whole point. It's what tells you big institutions are buying again. Without it, this is just a nice up day. Day six isn't too late either. It most often comes several days into a rally attempt. So I keep my list ready and wait for a day the volume shows up.
questions.lesson_line: Price and volume both have to show up. Half a signal isn't the signal.

wrong.Yes, the gain is big enough: Price alone doesn't do it. The day needs higher volume too.
wrong.Yes, any up day off a low counts: An up day alone isn't the signal. Early rallies often fail.
wrong.No, it's too late in the bounce: Timing's fine. It comes several days in, once a rally attempt is underway.

questions.simple: No, because a follow-through day needs a strong gain on higher volume, and volume fell.

reasons: the volume rule rests on one open source (StockCharts); IBD's rule pages are paywalled

questions.story: The index flushed on huge volume, then bounced. Now it's drifted back to that low. Volume's way lighter and the daily ranges are tight.
questions.q: What's this retest telling you?
choices: Constructive, sellers look spent
Bearish, light volume means no buyers
Meaningless, only price matters
Bearish, price is back at the low
questions.why: Constructive. Same price as the flush, but the selling's dried up. On the way down, sellers dumped stock on huge volume and wide ranges. Now they're barely showing up. That's what you want on a retest of a low: much lighter volume and narrow ranges. It says the sellers who wanted out are mostly gone. Don't marry it though. Several retests after a climax are common, and a quiet one is a test, not proof. Break the low with more stocks making new lows, and the bottom isn't in.
questions.lesson_line: A good retest is quiet. Same price, much less selling.

wrong.Bearish, light volume means no buyers: On a retest, light volume means few sellers. The worry is heavy selling or more stocks breaking down at the low.
wrong.Meaningless, only price matters: Volume is the tell on a retest. It shows if sellers are still pressing.
wrong.Bearish, price is back at the low: Price alone says little here. Volume and ranges shrank a lot, and that's what a good test looks like.

questions.simple: It looks good for buyers. Price is back at the low, but far fewer shares are being sold.

deeper.trap: A quiet retest is needed, but it is not enough. Wyckoff frames it as a condition: if a bottom is to be confirmed, volume and spread should shrink. That is not a promise. Several tests after a climax are common, so one quiet test settles nothing.

questions.q: From its 2022 low close of 3,577.03, what S&P 500 close makes a new bull market by the 20% rule? Round to a whole point.
questions.why: 4,292. A new bull is a 20% rise off the low, so multiply by 1.2. 3,577.03 times 1.2 is 4,292.44, which rounds to 4,292. The S&P 500 first closed that high on June 8, 2023, at 4,293.93. The low was almost eight months old by then. That's why I don't wait for the label. Winning stocks launch their big moves at the start of a new uptrend, not when the headlines make it official.
questions.lesson_line: The 20% rule makes a bull official late. By then the low is months old.
questions.simple: About 4,292, because a 20% gain from 3,577.03 means multiplying it by 1.2.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the 20% line as a buy signal. It is a label, and it comes late. The S&P 500's low close was 3,577.03 on Oct. 12, 2022, but it did not close above 4,292 until June 8, 2023. IBD says winning stocks launch their big moves at the start of a new market uptrend.

wrong.4,471: That undoes a 20% loss. A 20% gain from the low is times 1.2.
wrong.5,151: You added 20% twice. One 20% gain is the line.
wrong.4,650: That's a bigger rise than the 20% rule.

find.label: A new bull market closes at

questions.story: Six red days in a row. This morning a hotter-than-expected inflation report hits. The index drops as much as 2.4%, to a near two-year low. It closes up 2.6%.
questions.q: What do you make of that close?
choices: Bad news failed, a clue not proof
Likely a follow-through day, buy some
Bear rally, sell into the bounce
Probably noise, nothing to note
questions.answer: Bad news failed, a clue not proof
questions.why: Bad news failed, and that's worth noting. The worst headline you could ask for hit, and the index went from down 2.4% to up 2.6%. Even the analysts couldn't really explain it. When price stops falling on bad news, sellers may be running out. But it's day one of a rally attempt. So it's a clue, not a buy signal. This was the S&P 500, the day after its Oct. 12 low close in 2022. I'd mark that low and watch two things: does it hold, and does a follow-through day come.
questions.lesson_line: Watch how price reacts to bad news. When it stops falling on it, pay attention.

wrong.Bear rally, sell into the bounce: You can't know that yet. A bear rally only shows itself once it unwinds.
wrong.Likely a follow-through day, buy some: Too early. It just ended a six-day losing streak, so this is day one. A follow-through day comes several days in, on higher volume.
wrong.Probably noise, nothing to note: It's worth noting. Turns form while the headlines are still bad, and a big reversal on bad news is one clue.

questions.simple: Price shrugging off bad news is worth noting, but one day like this proves nothing on its own.

deeper.example: This was the S&P 500 in October 2022. The next day it closed at 3,583.07, right back near its Oct. 12 low close of 3,577.03. One reversal bar does not settle it. Watch whether the low holds, and whether a follow-through day comes later on higher volume.

questions.story: After a long slide, the index closes at 3,585.62. Two sessions later it's at 3,790.93.
questions.q: Is the low in?
choices: Not proven, early pops often fail
Yes, two days that strong confirm it
Likely, sellers look exhausted
Yes, that new low was capitulation
questions.answer: Not proven, early pops often fail
questions.why: Not proven. Two big days off a low feel great. But early rallies often fail and pull you right back into the decline. Two sessions is also too soon for a follow-through day. That comes several days into the attempt, on higher volume. This was the S&P 500, the end of September to Oct. 4, 2022. It went on to close at 3,577.03 on Oct. 12, the bear market's closing low. Buy that pop with size and you'd have given it all back. Let the market prove it first.
questions.lesson_line: The first pop off a low proves little. I let the market prove it.

wrong.Yes, two days that strong confirm it: Two days in is too early. A follow-through day comes several days into the attempt, on higher volume.
wrong.Likely, sellers look exhausted: That's only clear in hindsight. On Oct. 12 it closed at a new low of 3,577.03.
wrong.Yes, that new low was capitulation: Only the rebound confirms capitulation, and early calls are often wrong. On Oct. 12 it closed lower still, at 3,577.03.

questions.simple: Not yet. Early bounces often fail, and two strong days can't prove a bottom.

deeper.trap: The trap is a sharp pop right after a new low. Here the S&P 500 went from 3,585.62 at the end of September to 3,790.93 two sessions later. Then it closed at 3,577.03 on Oct. 12, a new low. Capitulation is only certain after the price has rebounded. Let the market prove the turn.

questions.story: This index fell more than 20% from its high. Then it rallied for two months off its low.
questions.q: Is the bear market over?
choices: Not proven. It may be a bear rally
Yes. A rally this big ends a bear
Yes. That low won't be broken now
No. It's sure to make new lows
questions.answer: Not proven. It may be a bear rally
questions.why: Not proven. There's no sure way to spot a bear rally until it unwinds. This was the S&P 500, from 3,666.77 on June 16 to 4,305.20 on Aug. 16, 2022, short of the 20% bull line. It closed at 3,577.03 on Oct. 12, below the June low.
questions.lesson_line: A big rally inside a bear proves nothing. I wait for the market to confirm the turn.

wrong.Yes. A rally this big ends a bear: Bear rallies can be huge, often on weak breadth. The Nasdaq ran 16% in two weeks that March and still made new lows.
wrong.Yes. That low won't be broken now: Nothing guarantees that. Here the index undercut the June low in October.
wrong.No. It's sure to make new lows: You can't be sure either way. No one can tell a bear rally until it unwinds.

questions.q: The VIX closed at 36.45 on March 7, 2022. On Oct. 12, the S&P 500's low close, it was 33.57. What's that telling you?
choices: Fear ran higher well before the low
Fear peaked on the day of the S&P low
VIX over 30 is a clear buy signal
Fear was gone by the October low
questions.answer: Fear ran higher well before the low
questions.why: Fear ran higher well before the low. The VIX closed at 36.45 on March 7, 2022. Seven months later, on the S&P 500's lowest close of the year, it was lower, at 33.57. So the bigger spike came seven months early, and it didn't mark the bottom. 2008 played out the same way. The VIX peaked late that year, and the S&P 500 didn't bottom until early March 2009. The VIX shows you an extreme. It doesn't time the low. I use a spike as one signpost, then wait for price to turn.
questions.lesson_line: A fear spike shows an extreme. It doesn't mark the low.

wrong.VIX over 30 is a clear buy signal: It was over 30 in March, and the S&P 500 didn't make its low close until Oct. 12. Spikes show extremes. They don't time the low.
wrong.Fear was gone by the October low: Not gone. The VIX closed at 33.57 that day, still over 30. Just lower than the 36.45 of March 7.
wrong.Fear peaked on the day of the S&P low: It didn't. The VIX closed at 33.57 that day, lower than the 36.45 of March 7.

questions.simple: Fear ran higher in March than at the October low, so a fear spike doesn't mark the bottom.

deeper.trap: The trap is buying an early VIX spike. In 2022 the VIX closed at 36.45 on March 7. The S&P 500's lowest close came months later, on Oct. 12, with the VIX lower, at 33.57. ChartSchool says volatility indices are not really predictive. They identify sentiment extremes.

reasons: closes from FRED (Tier 1) plus ChartSchool's 2008 example

questions.q: Oct. 2022: the S&P 500 undercut its summer low, but fewer stocks made new lows. What confirms that divergence?
choices: Price climbing back over that low
The Fed starting to cut interest rates
The VIX spiking back above 30 again
One more new low on heavy volume
questions.answer: Price climbing back over that low
questions.why: Price getting back above that low. The divergence was the clue. The index broke its June low, but most stocks didn't follow it. The proof was price. Once the S&P 500 climbed back above the June lows, the divergence was confirmed. That's how I treat any breadth clue. It tells me where to look. Price tells me when to act. And you didn't need the Fed to cut. It was still hiking in December.
questions.lesson_line: A divergence tells you where to look. Price getting back above the low tells you when.

wrong.The Fed starting to cut interest rates: No need to wait for that. The Fed was still hiking in December 2022. The proof was price, back above the June lows.
wrong.The VIX spiking back above 30 again: A fear spike shows an extreme, not a turn. It doesn't confirm anything.
wrong.One more new low on heavy volume: That's more selling, not a turn. The proof came when the index got back above its June lows.

questions.simple: Price getting back above the old June low is what confirmed the divergence.

deeper.example: In June 2022 the new low came with a multi-year high in stocks at 3-month lows. In October, fewer stocks made new lows. ChartSchool says strength like that can sometimes foreshadow a turn up, not always.

reasons: the key (what confirmed the divergence) rests on one CMT Association article; ChartSchool backs the divergence, not the confirmation
stem no longer names 'divergence' so it does not answer q04

questions.q: The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq put in their lowest 2022 closes on different days.
questions.why: True. The S&P 500's lowest close came Oct. 12, at 3,577.03. The Nasdaq kept going. On Dec. 28 it closed at 10,213.29, under its Oct. 12 close of 10,417.10. That same day the S&P 500 sat at 3,783.22, well above its low. Watch only one index and you'd have read the turn wrong. Bottoms are a process, and indexes can bottom weeks apart. Check both before you call a low. This is on closes. Intraday lows can land on other days.
questions.lesson_line: Bottoms are a process. Indexes can bottom weeks apart, so check more than one.
questions.simple: True. The S&P 500 had its low close in October 2022, while the Nasdaq closed lower in December.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the whole market off one index. On Dec. 28, 2022 the Nasdaq made a lower close than in October, at 10,213.29. The S&P 500 that day sat at 3,783.22, well above its Oct. 12 low close. Check more than one index before you call a low.

questions.story: A follow-through day just fired after a long decline. Your watch list from the correction has two kinds of names. Some held near their highs. Some got crushed.
questions.q: Where do you look first?
choices: Strong names breaking out of bases
The stocks that fell the most
Old leaders still far off their highs
Nothing yet, wait for a 20% rally
questions.answer: Strong names breaking out of bases
questions.why: The strong names breaking out of bases. The stocks that held up while the market fell are showing you relative strength. They tend to be the first to move when a new uptrend starts. O'Neil found the biggest winners get bought as they move up out of well-formed bases, not at their lows. So go down your list and find the ones near their highs with tight bases. Start with a few of the best breakouts, and take more names only as those work. The names that got crushed look cheap. They're cheap for a reason.
questions.lesson_line: Build the list in the correction. When the turn comes, start with the strongest names.

wrong.The stocks that fell the most: Big winners get bought as they move up out of bases, not at their lows.
wrong.Old leaders still far off their highs: Leaders show up as the strongest stocks right now. A name still far off its highs isn't acting like one.
wrong.Nothing yet, wait for a 20% rally: That waits way too long. The new bull wasn't official by the 20% rule until June 2023, and winners launch at the start of the uptrend.

questions.simple: Start with the strongest names breaking out of bases. Leaders tend to be the first to move off a low.

deeper.trap: The trap is buying what fell most because it looks cheap. O'Neil's research says the biggest winners are bought as they move higher out of well-formed bases, not at their lowest point. A stock that held near its highs through the correction is showing strength. That is the list to work first.

questions.story: You bought two leaders after a follow-through day. A week later the index undercuts its low, and more stocks hit new lows than last time.
questions.q: What's the read?
choices: Bottom isn't in. Cut back and protect
Add more. It's a cheaper entry
Hold. The follow-through day said buy
Short everything. The bear is back
questions.answer: Bottom isn't in. Cut back and protect
questions.why: Bottom isn't in. The CMT article says it plainly. A new low with internals worse than the prior low is a good signal the bottom isn't in yet. IBD says follow-through signals are not foolproof. In a correction, protect your gains and cut losses quickly. Keep the watch list ready for the next attempt.
questions.lesson_line: When the signal fails, I cut back fast and rebuild the watch list for the next one.

wrong.Add more. It's a cheaper entry: That's adding to a loser in a failing market. In a correction, cut losses quickly.
wrong.Hold. The follow-through day said buy: The signal can fail, and this one is failing. Follow-through days aren't foolproof.
wrong.Short everything. The bear is back: That swings to the other extreme. One failed signal doesn't tell you how far the decline runs. Protect capital and get your list ready.

questions.simple: The bottom is not in, since the index broke its low with more stocks breaking down, so protect your money first.

deeper.trap: The trap is loyalty to the signal. A follow-through day only shifts the odds, and IBD says it is not foolproof. When the index undercuts its low and more stocks hit new lows than last time, the market has changed its answer. Cut losses quickly and rebuild the watch list for the next attempt.

reasons: touches account behaviour the owner's rulebook governs (A4 stop is the exit, A5 no adding, F68); keyed on web sources only

questions.story: You bought two leaders after a follow-through day. A week later the index undercuts its low, and more stocks hit new lows than last time.
questions.q: What's going on, and what do you do with those two positions?
choices: Bottom isn't in, let your stops work
A cheaper entry, add to the leaders
Just a shakeout, lower your stops
The buy signal stands, cancel the stops
questions.answer: Bottom isn't in, let your stops work
questions.simple: The bottom isn't in, since the index broke its low with more stocks breaking down. Let your stops do their job.
questions.why: The bottom isn't in, so let your stops do their job. A new low with more stocks breaking down than last time is the market changing its answer. The follow-through day only shifted the odds, and this one is failing. Your stops are already in with the broker. If price hits them, you're out with a small loss. That's the whole point of setting them before you buy. Don't lower them and don't add. Our stop only moves up. Keep the list ready for the next attempt.
questions.lesson_line: When the signal fails, the stop is the exit. Then rebuild the list for the next one.

wrong.A cheaper entry, add to the leaders: Worse breadth at a new low says the bottom isn't in. And you never add to a trade going against you.
wrong.Just a shakeout, lower your stops: Worse breadth at the new low says the bottom isn't in. And our stop only moves up, never down.
wrong.The buy signal stands, cancel the stops: Follow-through days fail, and this one is failing. Every position keeps a real stop order with the broker.

deeper.trap: The trap is loyalty to the signal. A follow-through day only shifts the odds, and IBD says it is not foolproof. When the index undercuts its low with worse internals, the market has changed its answer. Our stop is the exit. Never lower it, and never add into a failing signal.

reasons: house rule (A4, A5, D41) keyed in a history lesson; replaces q25, whose cut-back key taught a web view the rulebook replaced
the read (bottom isn't in) rests on one CMT Association article

questions.q: When a rally attempt fails, it's fine to lower your stop and give the trade more room.
questions.simple: False. Our stop only moves up, never down or wider, so it can do its job as the exit.
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up. Never down, never wider. You set it before you bought, while you were calm and had no money on the line. Lowering it now is hoping, not trading. Early rallies off a low often fail, and the stop gets you out while the loss is still small. The one exception is a gap down through your stop. Then the first 30 minutes of that day decide the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: Our stop only moves up. When a rally attempt fails, the stop is the exit.

reasons: house rule (A4) taught here so the rung 9 scenario (q26) never tests a rule the lesson did not teach

questions.q: You're watching a sell-off for capitulation. Which day looks like it?
choices: A sharp drop on unusually heavy volume
A slow drift down on light volume
A tight range on unusually heavy volume
A sharp rally on light volume
questions.answer: A sharp drop on unusually heavy volume
questions.why: The sharp drop on unusually heavy volume. That's panic, everyone heading for the exit at once. On the chart it's a wide red bar with volume way above normal. Often price closes well off the low that day, because big buyers are soaking up the selling. That's the look of a washout. I mark that day's low. I'm not buying it yet. I want to see what happens when price comes back to test it.
questions.lesson_line: Big drop, huge volume, a close well off the low. That's the look of a washout.

wrong.A slow drift down on light volume: A quiet slide isn't panic selling. Capitulation shows heavy volume.
wrong.A tight range on unusually heavy volume: A selling climax shows wide ranges. A tight range means little selling pressure.
wrong.A sharp rally on light volume: A rally is the opposite move. Capitulation is a sharp drop.

questions.simple: Capitulation looks like panic, a sharp drop on unusually heavy volume, often closing well off the low.
